summary: Defines SNMP management objects that expose a RADIUS accounting client, which tracks usage of network service. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 4670.

eli5.summary: Meters on a device that sends usage records to a bookkeeper, so people can check that it is sending them properly.

subtitle: SNMP management for RADIUS accounting clients.

tldr.problem: Network operators needed visibility into RADIUS accounting clients (the devices sending usage records to billing servers) to monitor their health and troubleshoot connection issues.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines a Management Information Base (MIB) that exposes counters and statistics about RADIUS accounting clients, allowing SNMP management stations to query request and response statistics, timeouts, and errors.
tldr.outcome: Operators can now monitor RADIUS accounting clients using standard SNMP tools without custom instrumentation. This enables early detection of configuration problems and network issues.

today: RFC 4670 replaced this document with an updated RADIUS Accounting Client MIB.

sections.title: Managing RADIUS Accounting Clients
sections.content:
RADIUS (Remote Access Dialin User Service) accounting allows network devices to track how much service each user consumed (bandwidth, minutes, data transferred). Devices acting as RADIUS accounting clients (typically network access servers like routers and dial-up concentrators) send Accounting-Request packets to a RADIUS accounting server, which replies with Accounting-Response. The accounting server collects this data for billing and reporting.

This document defines a Management Information Base (MIB) that exposes RADIUS accounting client statistics, allowing a network management station (using SNMP) to monitor and troubleshoot RADIUS accounting clients. The MIB covers request and response counts, timeouts, authentication failures, and malformed packets.
sections.eli5: RADIUS is a bookkeeping system: devices report how much they used to a server. Network managers need to see if the reports are being sent correctly, so this defines meters they can read.

sections.title: The SNMP Management Framework and MIB Structure
sections.content:
The MIB is defined using SMIv2 (Structure of Management Information version 2), which is compliant with SNMPv3. It can be translated to SMIv1 for use with older SNMP versions. The MIB exposes managed objects that can be queried and retrieved by SNMP management stations.

The MIB module contains two scalar values and one table: the RADIUS Accounting Server Table, which has one row for each RADIUS accounting server that the client communicates with. Each table entry includes thirteen columns presenting statistics about requests, responses, retransmissions, timeouts, errors, and authentication failures for that server.
sections.eli5: The MIB is a list of numbers (called "objects") that SNMP can read. It has overall counters and a table with one row per accounting server, showing request and response statistics.

sections.title: Key Managed Objects and Statistics
sections.content:
The MIB defines an identifier for the client (radiusAccClientIdentifier) and a counter for invalid server addresses (packets received from unknown sources). For each accounting server, it tracks: the server's IP address and UDP port, round-trip time to the server, the number of Accounting-Requests sent (excluding retransmissions), retransmissions, responses received, malformed responses, responses with bad authenticators, pending requests, timeouts, unknown-type packets, and dropped packets.

The relationship between these counters is: Requests = Responses + PendingRequests + Timeouts. Similarly, successfully received packets = Responses - (MalformedResponses + BadAuthenticators + UnknownTypes + PacketsDropped). These formulas allow operators to validate data consistency and identify specific failure modes.
sections.eli5: The meters track sent requests, received responses, retries, timeouts, and errors. By comparing them, managers can see if the client and server are in sync and spot problems like lost packets or bad authentication.

sections.title: Monitoring and Troubleshooting with the MIB
sections.content:
Network operators use SNMP to query these counters periodically, creating trends and alerts. A spike in timeouts indicates the server may be unreachable or overloaded. A rise in malformed-response or bad-authenticator counters suggests a misconfiguration (wrong shared secret) or a compromised server. A high pending-requests count indicates the server is not responding in time.

Since there are no read-write or read-create objects in this MIB, direct SNMP SET operations cannot alter client behavior. All objects are read-only, making the MIB purely observational. This prevents accidental misconfiguration via SNMP.
sections.eli5: Managers watch these numbers over time. If timeouts jump up, the server might be down. If errors appear, something is misconfigured. High pending counts mean the server is slow to respond.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
Some objects in the MIB contain sensitive information. The radiusAccServerAddress reveals where the accounting server is located; an attacker could use this to mount a denial-of-service attack on the server. The radiusAccClientServerPortNumber reveals which port the client uses; an attacker could attempt to impersonate the client.

SNMPv1 provides no built-in security. Even on a secure network, there is no mechanism to control who can read these objects. SNMPv3, with the User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575), allows administrators to grant read access only to trusted principals. This is the recommended approach.
sections.eli5: The server's address and port are secrets that could help an attacker. So network managers should use SNMPv3, which lets them decide who can read these numbers and encrypts the data in transit.
